items.title: 10.10.2 Calculating the charge on an electron

source_refs.note: Topic 10.10.2, printed pages 223-224. The print treats 99646 C (charge per mole of copper) as the charge on a mole of electrons; kept as printed and noted.

blocks.text: A sample calculation uses a current of 0.20 A for 34 min. Mass of anode at the start 56.53 g, at the end 56.40 g, so the copper removed is 0.13 g. The charge passed is Q = I x t = 0.20 x 34 x 60 = 408 C. Since 0.13 g of copper requires 408 C, 1 g requires 408 / 0.13 C, and 63.5 g (1 mole) requires 408 / 0.13 x 63.5 = 99646 C. The electrolysis equation Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s) shows that 2 moles of electrons are needed per mole of copper. The print then takes the charge on 1 mole of electrons as 99646 C (this is in fact the charge per mole of copper, two moles of electrons; the slip is kept as printed). With the charge on one electron 1.60 x 10^-19 C, L = 99646 / (1.60 x 10^-19) = 6.2 x 10^23 mol-1, in good agreement with the accurate value 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1.

blocks.prompt: A current of 0.500 A for 30.0 min deposits 0.503 g of silver (molar mass 107.87 g mol-1, Ag+). Calculate Avogadro's number from this data (exercise Q.2j).
blocks.explanation: Q = 0.500 x 1800 = 900 C. Moles of silver = 0.503 / 107.87 = 4.66 x 10^-3 mol, each needing one electron, so the charge per mole of electrons is 900 / 4.66 x 10^-3 = 1.93 x 10^5 C. Dividing by 1.60 x 10^-19 C gives NA = 1.2 x 10^24 mol-1, about twice the accepted value, which shows the silver mass in the question is inconsistent with the charge; with the accepted Faraday 96500 C the data would give 0.1006 g of silver.

items: 0.20 A for 34 min: 408 C removes 0.13 g Cu, so 63.5 g needs 99646 C; dividing by the electron charge 1.60 x 10^-19 C gives L = 6.2 x 10^23 mol-1 (accurate 6.02 x 10^23).
